newsitem.title: UK: British scientists make advance on CJD disease.
newsitem.headline: British scientists make advance on CJD disease.

text.p: British scientists worried about a new variant of CJD, the human version of "mad cow" disease, said on Friday they had identified a simple technique which they expected would allow early diagnosis.

The discovery could help prevent panic if Britain faced an epidemic as a result of people having eaten beef from cows suffering from Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), they wrote in the British medical journal The Lancet.
So far 14 cases of the new variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (nvCJD) have been confirmed in Britain, where mad cow disease has been prevalent in cattle, and one in France.
But the scientists from London's Imperial College School of Medicine said an epidemic was possible if theories that nvCJD is linked to eating contaminated beef years earlier were confirmed.
"It is at present unclear how many further cases of nvCJD are likely to appear," they noted.
But they added: "If nvCJD is caused by BSE, and an epidemic ensues, early diagnostic markers will be essential for differential diagnosis."
"The present clinical features (depression and sensory disturbance) are non-specific and many may be concerned that they have developed this condition."
In the past, confirmation that a patient has nvCJD has been possible only through a dangerous brain biopsy before death or a post-mortem examination.

The scientists reported they had discovered that a prion protein found in the brains of people suffering from nvCJD was also present in the tonsil tissue of a 35-year-old woman who had died from the disease.
This suggested it was possible to check for nvCJD through a simple and safe procedure under local anaesthetic, which would be viable even for people who have had their tonsils out.
But John Collinge, head of the Imperial College team, said further research was needed to assess how useful the new technique will be.
"We now need to extend this initial study and see how early in the disease this marker may be useful," he said.
